attest

uh-TEST -- stress on the second syllable, TEST. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To attest is to certify or serve as clear evidence that something is true.

The championship trophies lining the hallway attest to decades of dedicated coaching.

Example

The notary watches the couple sign the deed, then adds her own signature and seal to attest that she saw it happen.

By signing, the notary attests to the signatures -- she formally certifies, from direct knowledge, that they are genuine. To attest to something is to serve as a witness or as clear evidence that it is true.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

verify: To verify is to check something yourself until you are sure it is true -- recounting the ballots, testing the lock, comparing the records. Attest points the other way: you attest to what you already know or what the evidence shows, backing its truth for others rather than checking it for yourself.

witness: To witness is to see an event happen with your own eyes. Attest reaches further: a witness merely saw it, while to attest is to formally back its truth afterward -- and a document or an object can attest to something, though only a person can witness it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dispute: to argue that something is not true

refute: to prove a claim false

Where it sits · how formally you back the claim — affirm → attest → testify

affirm vs. attest: Affirm is lighter than attest -- to affirm is simply to say in words that something is true, while to attest is to back the claim as evidence or a witness, often from direct knowledge.

testify vs. attest: Testify is the most formal of the family: you attest to something whenever you certify it is true, but you testify under oath, in court, where your words carry legal consequences.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — at- (ad-)

prefix — at- (ad-): to, toward (Latin)

root — test-

root — test-: witness (Latin testis)

Put it together

Put it together: Attest comes from Latin ad- ('to') plus testis ('witness') -- literally 'to be a witness to.' When records, scars, or people attest to something, they stand as witnesses whose very existence backs up the claim.

Use the root in a new word: testimony

Use the root in a new word: testimony: The jury listened closely to the shopkeeper's testimony about the night of the break-in.

Root Check

Word Choice

Attest usually takes 'to': witnesses attest to what they saw, and records attest to what happened. Note that objects and documents can attest just as well as people -- a stamped passport attests to a journey. It is a favorite of formal reports and recommendation letters.
